682d01a273:
This chapter walks through, from first principles, the loop that turns a stateless text predictor into an agent. You'll see what the model actually returns, why it stops, and what goes over the wire on every turn. You'll see how the conversation history becomes the agent's only memory. And you'll see why the loop must be steered by stop_reason and nothing else.

The story runs from rule engines and decision trees, through ReAct and function calling, to the SDK tool runner and the Claude Agent SDK. Implementations are in Python and Java/Spring.
6e4ab2100b:
The whole topic collapses into two sentences.

A model call returns exactly one assistant message and then forgets everything, so an agent is your code calling the model repeatedly, running the tools it asks for, and appending every request and result to a history that you resend each time.

The loop continues while stop_reason is "tool_use" and ends when it is "end_turn"; the decision of what to do next belongs to the model, and the decision of when the loop is over belongs to that structured field, never to the wording of the reply or a turn counter.
84656d5989:
Everything else in this chapter follows from those two sentences.

The wire format (tool_use ids, tool_result pairing, ordering rules) exists because the API is stateless. It has to be able to check that a history is coherent. The cost curve, with input tokens growing every turn, exists because the history is resent.

The three anti-patterns the exam names are three ways of swapping the structured stop signal for something weaker: the meaning of words, the presence of text, or a number you picked.

And the Agent SDK, Claude Code and every "harness" you'll meet in later chapters are this same loop with more machinery bolted on: permissions, hooks, context compaction, subagents.
6c9a007416:
The official task statement for 1.1 lists four knowledge points. You need to recognise each one in an exam scenario, and in code:

  • the loop lifecycle: send a request, inspect stop_reason, execute tools, return results for the next iteration;
  • tool results are appended to the conversation history, so the model can reason over them;
  • the difference between model-driven decision-making and pre-configured decision trees;
  • three anti-patterns: parsing natural-language signals to decide termination, using arbitrary iteration caps as the primary stopping mechanism, and checking assistant text content as a completion indicator.

Domain 1 carries the largest weight in the exam. Almost every other task statement in it (coordinators and subagents, hooks, sessions, enforcement) sits on top of this loop. Know exactly what crosses the wire on each turn, and questions about subagents or hooks become questions about which step of this loop is being changed.
044168b29e:
If you've built sagas in Spring, hold on to this analogy. We'll test it as we go: the harness is a saga orchestrator.

Each model response is an event. The orchestrator reads its type (stop_reason), not its free-text log line, to decide what to do next. The messages array is the saga log that lets the process resume and be audited.

The difference from a Spring State Machine is where the transition table lives. In a classic saga, you wrote the transitions. In an agentic loop, the model chooses the next step from the facts so far. Your code only enforces the protocol and the guardrails.
7ccf2a85d0: Agentic loops didn't appear out of nowhere in 2023. Every piece of today's design answers a limitation of something earlier. Trace that lineage, and it becomes obvious why the exam keeps returning to one idea: let the model decide the path, and let structured signals decide termination.
f157225d03:
The first serious attempt to automate expert decisions was the expert system.

MYCIN at Stanford (mid-1970s) diagnosed blood infections with roughly 600 hand-written IF-THEN rules and a backward-chaining inference engine. XCON at DEC configured VAX computers with thousands of rules, and saved the company millions a year.

The architecture was a knowledge base of rules plus an engine that decided which rule fired next. The engine was deterministic and auditable. That's still why rule engines like Drools sit inside telecom order management and credit decisioning today.
87e07aa2b0:
The failure mode was just as clear. Every path had to be anticipated by a person. When a case combined two problems, or used a phrase nobody had written a rule for, the system either fell through to a default branch or gave a confident wrong answer.

Maintenance grew with the square of the rules, because new rules interacted with old ones. Researchers called this the knowledge acquisition bottleneck: the system could only be as good as the tree someone had time to write.
a631aca847:
Customer service automation inherited the same structure. A phone IVR ("press 1 for billing") is a decision tree with a voice.

The chatbot platforms of the 2010s replaced the keypad with an intent classifier. A model maps the user's sentence to one of a fixed set of intents ("billing_dispute", "activation_issue"). Then a hand-built dialog tree takes over, filling slots and calling backend APIs at pre-wired nodes. Machine learning did the routing. Humans still wrote the path.
d658b3ae0c:
Anyone who has worked on a telecom contact-centre platform knows the result. A ticket that contains two problems gets classified as one. The tree handles that one, and the customer calls back.

The classifier is single-shot: it decides once, up front. And the tree can't change its mind after it has seen data. Section 11 replays exactly this failure against a model-driven loop.
b1b55fc354:
GPT-3 (2020) showed that a large language model could do many tasks from instructions and a few examples in the prompt. In 2022, chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al.) showed that asking the model to write out intermediate reasoning steps improved multi-step problem solving.

But a model on its own can only produce text from what's in its context window. It can't look up an order, read today's outage list, or issue a refund. Its knowledge is frozen at training time, and it has no hands.
64812e85b0:
The paper that named the pattern was ReAct (Yao et al., 2022, "Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models").

The idea was to prompt the model to alternate three kinds of lines: Thought (reasoning about what to do), Action (a call such as Search[Verizon 5G home outage]), and Observation (the result, pasted in by the surrounding program).

The program watched the generated text. When it saw an Action line, it stopped the model, ran the action, appended the Observation, and called the model again. That's the agentic loop, already complete in 2022: generate, detect a request, execute, append the result, generate again.
399b047571:
What ReAct lacked was a structured contract. The harness found the action by parsing text with regular expressions. It decided the task was over when the model wrote a line like Finish[answer]. Both are natural-language signals.

So when the model formatted an action slightly differently, wrote "Finish" inside a thought, or never wrote it at all, the harness broke.

The first and third anti-patterns in the exam (parsing natural language for termination, checking text for completion) are, quite literally, the ReAct-era harness. The industry spent the next two years removing them.
5337fb0bc3:
Toolformer (Schick et al., early 2023) showed that models could be trained to decide for themselves when to call an API, and with what arguments.

The same year, model providers moved tool calling out of the prompt and into the API. You no longer asked the model to write Action: lookup_order[ORD-118204] and then scraped it. Instead, you declared tools with a name, a description and a JSON Schema for the input. The model returned a structured tool call: a typed object with a name and a JSON argument object, separate from any prose.

The response also carried a machine-readable reason for stopping. Parsing disappeared from the harness. Now it reads fields.
fcee1d01b4:
Anthropic's Messages API gained tool use in spring 2024 (as a beta, generally available shortly after). Its design is the one this chapter dissects:

  • tools are declared in the request;
  • the model returns tool_use content blocks, each with an id, a name and an input object;
  • the response says stop_reason: "tool_use";
  • your next request carries tool_result blocks that reference those ids.

Later that year, the Model Context Protocol (MCP, November 2024) standardised how tools are provided to a model application: servers expose tools, resources and prompts over a common protocol. So the same tool implementation can plug into many hosts.

MCP changes where tool definitions come from. It doesn't change the loop. Domain 2 of this guide covers it.
538c667251:
Once every team was writing the same loop, the loop itself became a product.

Claude Code is a harness: the agentic loop plus file and shell tools, permission prompts, hooks that run before and after tool calls, context compaction, and subagents. Anthropic then exposed that harness as a library. It started as the Claude Code SDK and was renamed the Claude Agent SDK. With it, you run the same loop in your own process, with your own tools. The client SDKs also gained a lighter tool runner that wraps the bare loop around plain functions. Section 14 shows both.

The point for the exam: these are packaged versions of this chapter's loop, not different mechanisms. They all still branch on stop_reason, append results to history, and treat iteration limits as safety budgets.
7e15312547:
To see why stop_reason is the right control signal, you need to know what happens inside a single call.

A transformer language model is a function from a sequence of tokens to a probability distribution over the next token. Generation is a loop inside the API. It tokenizes your request (system prompt, tool definitions, every message). It runs the model to get a distribution, samples one token, appends it, and runs again. And again. Each new token is computed from everything before it.

Nothing about the call persists afterwards: no session, no cursor, no hidden memory. When generation stops, the server packages the tokens into content blocks and returns them.
979f1e242c:
The first two are the normal cases, and the only ones the official task statement names. The rest are operational edge cases. A production loop must still handle them, because treating any of them as "done" hands the user a broken answer.

At the time of writing, the Python SDK's StopReason type lists exactly these seven values. Check the API reference when you build, because new values get added as features ship.
dc5126c7ed:
Notice what's missing from that table: any reference to the content of the reply.

The model may write "Done!" and still have stop_reason: "tool_use", because it also requested a tool. It may write a long paragraph that sounds unfinished and still end with end_turn.

The structured field is generated by the server from what actually happened in the token loop. The words are generated by the model to talk to a human. Only one of them is a protocol.
fa6fb110c3:
Before writing a loop, look at the exact bytes. Everything that goes wrong in a harness shows up first as a malformed request.

We'll trace one tool round trip for a support agent. A customer writes: "What's the status of ORD-220871?" The harness has one relevant tool, lookup_order. (Companion: 02_one_tool_round_trip.py.)
800ab176c2:
Three parts deserve attention.

system and tools are top-level fields, not messages. They're part of every request you send, and they're tokens you pay for on every call.

The tool description is the only thing the model knows about when and how to use the tool. That's why Domain 2 spends a whole task statement on writing them.

And messages starts with a user turn, because the API requires the conversation to begin with the user role.
88474731ba:
Behind the scenes, the API renders the tool definitions into a special section of the prompt that the model was trained to read. It also adds a tool-use system preamble. That preamble costs a few hundred extra input tokens per request whenever tools are present. (The exact number varies by model and tool_choice; check the pricing docs.)

This is the first hint that tool definitions aren't free. Twenty verbose tools, sent on every turn of a ten-turn loop, are a real line on the bill.
7a2f2a8721:
The response is one assistant message whose content is an array of blocks, not a string. Here it holds a text block (a short preamble, which Claude often writes before acting) and a tool_use block.

The tool_use block has three fields that matter:

  • id is a server-generated identifier, unique within the conversation. The result must reference it.
  • name is one of the tools you declared.
  • input is an already-parsed JSON object that the model generated to match your input_schema.

With strict tool schemas enabled, input is guaranteed to validate. Without them, it usually does. Either way, your tool should validate its input as you would any request body.
3fc42a8eba:
Then comes stop_reason: "tool_use". The model has stopped, and it's waiting.

If you returned the text block to the user now, they'd see "Let me check that order." and nothing else. If you threw this response away and called again with the original messages, the model would ask for the same tool again. Nothing in the history says it was ever run.
4c4f820ca0:
This is the heart of the protocol. The second request contains, in order:

  • the first request's messages, unchanged;
  • the assistant turn, exactly as received;
  • a new user message whose content is a tool_result block.

The tool_use_id equals the id from the tool_use block. A tool result's content can be a string (here, a JSON string) or an array of content blocks: text, and images for tools that return screenshots or documents. There's also an optional is_error boolean, which section 09 covers.
004204beec:
Why does a tool result travel in a user message? Because the conversation model has only two speakers. Anything that isn't the model speaking is input to the model, and the API models that as the user role.

It's the tool_result block type, not the role, that tells the model "this is the output of the call you asked for".
b2dd19b3f4:
end_turn: the model has what it needs, and it has answered.

Input tokens went from 612 to 738, because the second request carried the first exchange plus the tool result. That growth is the cost model of every agent. Section 07 works it out.
e189bc6356:
Generalise the round trip, and you have the agentic loop. The task statement describes its lifecycle in four steps: send a request to Claude, inspect stop_reason, execute the requested tools, and return their results for the next iteration.

In code, that's a while True whose only normal exit is a stop reason other than tool_use.
aebd10b653: The assistant turn is appended before anything else, and verbatim. We append resp.content, the SDK's list of block objects, without rebuilding it. The SDK serialises those objects back into the same JSON on the next request. Rebuilding the turn by hand (keeping only the text, say) is how ids, thinking signatures and ordering get lost.
c9d283836d:
Here's the trace of that loop on the support scenario used throughout the companion code.

The customer writes: "My order ORD-118204 arrived with a cracked screen. I want my money back." Four tools are available: lookup_order, check_refund_policy, issue_refund (which refuses amounts above 500.00) and escalate_to_human. The system prompt says refunds above 500 must be escalated. (Run python 03_agentic_loop.py --mock.)
3f885855df:
Step through it as the model would.

Turn 1. The model knows only the customer's sentence and the tool list. The cheapest way to make progress is to look up the order.

Turn 2. It has the order (a 799.00 phone, delivered six days ago), and asks whether that SKU and reason are refundable.

Turn 3. Policy says yes, and the model tries to issue the refund. In this run, the model attempted the refund even though the system prompt says to escalate above 500. Real models usually respect such instructions. But "usually" is the point, and the tool itself enforces the limit and returns an error.

Turn 4. The model reads the error, changes plan, and escalates.

Turn 5. It has a ticket number, and writes the answer.
46fd0b13bb:
Nobody wrote "if refund fails, escalate" anywhere in the harness. The model chose that path one step at a time, from the facts the loop appended. That is what the exam means by model-driven decision-making. Section 11 sets it against the alternative.

The trace also shows a division of labour. The model chose to escalate. The tool guaranteed that no refund above 500 could be issued. When a rule must hold every time, put it in code (Domain 1, task 1.4 and hooks in 1.5), not only in the prompt.
30af7899be: The task statement's second knowledge point: tool results are appended to the conversation history so the model can reason about the next action. It sounds obvious. Its consequences run deep, and the exam tests several of them.
284bc2e87d:
Each call to the Messages API is independent. The server does not keep your conversation between calls. There is no session id to pass.

Prompt caching, covered in Domain 5, lets the server reuse work on a prefix it saw recently. That saves cost and latency. It is not memory: you still send the full prefix.

Companion example 01_single_call.py shows the obvious consequence. Ask a follow-up without history, and the model has no idea what "it" refers to.
b9f5b81105:
For an agent, this means three things.

  • First, the model can only reason over what is in messages. If you don't append a tool result, the model doesn't know the tool ran. It will usually ask for it again. If the tool has side effects (a refund, a port-out, an SMS), you have now done it twice.
  • Second, the history is the audit log. To explain why the agent did something, you replay messages.
  • Third, persistence is your job. The agent may need to survive a process restart, a pod eviction or a handover between services. Then you store messages (plus system prompt and tool definitions) somewhere durable.

Session resumption in Claude Code and the Agent SDK (task 1.7) is exactly this: the harness wrote the transcript to disk.
499124ccbb: A Spring architect knows this move. It is the same as making a service stateless behind a load balancer. The request carries everything needed to process it, and state lives in an external store. The difference: here the "request" grows on every call.
1df6de7dad: The server cannot remember what it asked for. So it validates the history you send. The rules are few and strict:
6736a24467: Every tool_use block in an assistant message needs a tool_result with the same id. That result goes in the immediately following user message.
9ae6b85d71: Every tool_result must reference a tool_use id in the immediately preceding assistant message. You cannot answer an older call. You cannot invent ids.
dd36876436: In that user message, tool_result blocks come first. Any text you add goes after them. An example is a new instruction the user typed while tools ran.
dd14cb56d2: Break a rule and the API rejects the request with HTTP 400 invalid_request_error. The model never runs. Companion example 05_pairing_errors.py reproduces the common bugs against the fake client, which enforces the same rules. Its output, abridged:
ff8d5023aa:
The two messages quoted in full follow the wording of the real API errors. The fake's message for the ordering rule is paraphrased.

Read the error paths. messages.2 is the index in your array. That is the fastest way to find the bad turn in a long history.

The "split across two user messages" case is accepted. The API merges consecutive messages with the same role into one turn. Don't rely on that. Write one user message per tool round, and the history stays easy to reason about and to persist.
aef35c305f:
This "missing result" bug has a subtle production form. The loop is interrupted (a timeout, a deploy) at a bad moment. The assistant turn with a tool_use was persisted, but the result was not. When the session resumes, the very first request is a 400.

Resumption code must do one of two things. Drop the dangling assistant turn, or execute it and answer it.

Cancelled tasks need the same care. If a user cancels mid-tool, append a tool_result with is_error: true and content like "cancelled by user". The history then stays valid.
c23d76c7d5:
One assistant turn can contain several tool_use blocks. Claude does this when the calls are independent. It might look up two orders, or fetch the bill breakdown and the device activation status at once.

The rules above already cover this. Execute all the calls and return all results in one user message. The results need not follow the order of the calls, because the ids carry the pairing. Keeping the order makes logs easier to read.
6b7e93852a: The calls are independent, so a harness can execute them concurrently. In Python, a thread pool is enough for I/O-bound tools. In Java, use a virtual-thread executor or CompletableFuture.allOf. Companion example 04_parallel_tool_calls.py:
99e39e01d9:
Two cautions.

First, "independent" is the model's judgement. Some tools have side effects that must run in order: reserve stock, then charge the card. Don't run them concurrently just because they arrived together. Either serialise side-effecting tools in the harness, or set disable_parallel_tool_use: true inside tool_choice. That tells the model to request at most one tool per turn.

Second, parallel calls change the shape of the trace, not the termination logic. The turn still has stop_reason: "tool_use". The loop still continues until a turn arrives that does not.
faef7bd53c:
Take the phrase "so the model can reason about the next action" literally. When the model generates turn 4 of the refund trace, its input contains:

  • the customer message;
  • its own earlier reasoning text;
  • the order record;
  • the policy result;
  • its failed refund attempt;
  • the error text "exceeds the 500.00 limit; needs supervisor approval".

The next-token distribution is conditioned on all of it. The word "supervisor" appears in the error. An escalate_to_human tool sits in the definitions. Together they make a call to that tool the likely continuation.

That is the mechanism of model-driven control. It is not a rule. It is conditioning on accumulated evidence.

It is also why the content of tool results matters so much. An error that says "PermissionError" and nothing else gives the model little to work with. An error that names the limit hit and what to do instead gives it much more.
2ae83b924f:
Statelessness has a price, and you can calculate it before you ship. Every call re-sends the system prompt, the tool definitions and the whole history. Define three quantities:

  • B: the fixed part of each request (system prompt plus tool definitions plus the tool-use preamble);
  • U: the user's opening message;
  • d: the tokens one tool round adds to the history (the assistant turn with its tool_use blocks, plus the user turn with the results).

Then the input of call k is roughly:
7a27f6e4d6:
The first term is linear in the number of calls. The second is quadratic. In short loops, the fixed part dominates. In long loops with large tool results, the quadratic term takes over.

That term is driven by d, and d is mostly the size of what your tools return. This is the strongest argument for two pieces of advice. Domain 2 says to return only the fields the model needs. Domain 5 covers context-management techniques. Trimming tool output cuts cost on every later turn, not just one.
52a30659a4:
Here is a worked example with round numbers.

  • B = 2,000 tokens (a system prompt and eight tool definitions);
  • U = 50;
  • each assistant turn: 100 tokens;
  • each tool result: either 800 tokens (a raw order-service JSON response) or 200 tokens (the same data trimmed to the fields the model uses).
77c11761a2:
Turn those into money with the current per-million-token prices for your model. Prices change, so read them from the pricing page and keep them in configuration, not code.

Take illustrative prices of 3 dollars per million input tokens and 15 per million output tokens. The 10-call raw run costs about 0.18 dollars of input and about 0.015 of output. That is roughly 20 cents a ticket.

At a million tickets a month, that is 200,000 dollars. Trimming the tool output saves about 80,000 of it. The numbers are illustrative. The shape is not.
d885a83ae5:
Two other levers change the curve.

Prompt caching lets the API reuse the processed prefix of a request it saw recently. Cached input is billed at a fraction of the normal input price: around a tenth at the time of writing (check the docs). An agentic loop is close to the ideal caching workload. Each request is the previous request plus a suffix.

That only works if the history is append-only. Each of these invalidates the cache from that point on: rewriting an earlier message, reordering tools, putting a timestamp in the system prompt.

Fewer, better turns is the other lever. Compare one tool that answers the question in one call ("get_refund_eligibility(order_id)") with three tools ("get_order", "get_sku", "get_policy"). The single tool cuts n, and n is the variable that is squared.
ec6df2c65f: Companion example 08_token_growth.py runs a loop whose tool returns 40 call-detail records each time. It prints per-turn and cumulative usage from resp.usage. In mock mode, token counts are estimates from request size. The curve still has the real shape:
c75c92ff42: The task statement focuses on tool_use and end_turn. Exam questions about the basic loop use only those two. A production loop needs an answer for the other values too. Treat any of them as "the model is done", and you get a specific, nasty bug.
743b7e2faf:
max_tokens bites most often. Suppose the model was mid-way through writing a tool_use block when the budget ran out. The input object may be incomplete.

  • Execute it, and you run a tool with arguments the model did not finish choosing.
  • Return the text, and you return half a sentence as an answer.

The handler above discards the truncated turn and retries with a bigger budget, a bounded number of times. For long-form text (not tool calls), you could instead append the partial turn and ask the model to continue. For tool calls, the clean retry is safer.

Set max_tokens generously in agent loops. You pay for tokens generated, not for the limit.
532e4bedc9:
pause_turn appears with server-side tools, where Anthropic runs the tool (web search, for example) inside the API call. A long turn can be paused and handed back.

The fix: send the response back as the assistant turn and call again. The server picks up where it stopped. Treat it as end_turn, and you return a partial answer. Treat it as tool_use, and you find no client tool to run.
550fce7b6b: refusal means a safety intervention stopped the reply. Retrying the same input in a loop is wasteful. In a customer-facing system, it can also look like probing. Surface it.
08aa1e9270: model_context_window_exceeded says the history no longer fits. The fix is architectural: compaction, summarising old tool results, or splitting work across subagents with their own contexts. The guide covers all three later.
0793fa364a: Unknown values must fail closed. The API adds stop reasons as features ship. A loop with an else: return text branch will one day return a non-answer as success. Companion example 07_stop_reasons.py runs each case against the fake client and prints the path taken.
c9a3675ba1: Tools fail. Order services time out. Inputs fail validation. Business rules reject requests. Permissions are missing. When a tool raises, a loop has three options. Only one is right.
95d365f92c: Let the exception escape. The loop crashes and the customer gets an HTTP 500. The history, and the model's partial work, is lost. Companion example 06_tool_errors.py shows this on the 799.00 refund: LOOP CRASHED: PermissionError.
01e5e6b95b: Swallow it and return something that looks normal, such as an empty string or {}. The model then believes the call succeeded. It may tell the customer "your refund has been issued". This is the worst option, because it is silent.
d7f491a346: Return a tool_result with is_error: true and a message the model can act on. The loop continues. The model reads the error and changes plan. In the refund trace, it escalated.
bfc9d53488:
is_error does not change the protocol. The result is still paired by id, and the loop still continues on tool_use. What changes is how the model reads the result.

Claude is trained to treat an error result as a failed attempt. It will typically do one of three things: retry with corrected input (after a validation error), try another tool, or explain the problem to the user.

So write error content for that reader. Say which input was wrong. Say what the limit is. Say whether retrying could help.

Task 2.2 of the exam covers structured error responses in detail: error categories, retryable flags. The loop-level rule is simpler: every tool_use gets a tool_result, success or failure, and failures carry is_error.
5e92413205:
Two harness-level decisions sit next to this.

Where do retries live? Retry transient infrastructure errors (a 503 from the order service) inside the tool, with backoff. That is exactly what you would do with Resilience4j in Spring. The model does not need to see a blip. Send business and validation errors to the model, because it can do something different.

Are your tools idempotent? The same call can run twice in several ways. The model may call the tool twice. A crashed loop may resume and re-run the last call. A parallel batch may be retried.

So side-effecting tools (refunds, SIM swaps, port-outs, account changes) should accept an idempotency key, as issue_refund does in the companion code. A replay then returns the original result instead of acting twice. You already know this distributed-systems rule. Here it applies to a new kind of client.
18af50f3c5:
With extended thinking on, Claude writes reasoning into thinking content blocks before its answer or tool calls. Each thinking block carries a signature. This opaque cryptographic value lets the API verify that the thinking you send back is the thinking it produced. The API may also return redacted_thinking blocks, whose content is encrypted. Treat them the same way.

Why this matters in a tool loop: the turn that requested the tool begins with a thinking block. After the tool result arrives, the model's reasoning must continue from that block.
857c29035d:
The rule: when you send tool results back, include the preceding assistant turn unmodified, thinking blocks and signatures included. Append resp.content as-is, as the canonical loop does, and you comply automatically.

The bug appears when someone tampers with history. They "clean it up". They rebuild turns from text. They filter out block types they don't recognise. Or they store only text in a database and rebuild messages from it. Companion example 15_thinking_in_loops.py strips the signature and gets the 400:
a3523c700e:
Two more constraints held at the time of writing. Check the extended-thinking docs for your model.

  • With thinking on, tool_choice supports only auto and none. You cannot force a specific tool on a thinking turn.
  • Thinking tokens count as output tokens toward max_tokens and cost. A loop with thinking needs a larger output budget per turn.

History persisted for resumption must store whole content blocks, not just text. Otherwise a resumed thinking conversation fails on its first request.
48eb95d63f:
Streaming delivers the response as server-sent events, in this order:

  1. message_start.
  2. For each content block: a content_block_start, then a series of deltas, then a content_block_stop. The deltas are text_delta for text, input_json_delta for fragments of a tool call's JSON input, and thinking_delta.
  3. message_delta, carrying the stop_reason and usage.
  4. message_stop.

Streaming lets you show text to a user as it is produced. It also avoids HTTP timeouts on long generations.
bfc924002a:
For the loop, this has two consequences. First, stop_reason arrives at the end of the stream, so you cannot branch until the stream finishes. Second, a tool call's input arrives as JSON fragments. They are not valid JSON until content_block_stop. Never run a tool from a partial input.

The SDKs collect the events for you. In Python, stream.get_final_message() returns the complete Message, identical to what create() would have returned. The rest of the loop is unchanged:
88888869ee: (Some SDK helpers can start a tool as soon as its block is complete, before the rest of the turn finishes streaming. The tool runner exposes this as an option. It is an optimisation on the same protocol. The result still goes back in the next user message, paired by id.)
93e0f230f6:
The third knowledge point asks you to tell apart two ways of deciding what happens next.

  • In a pre-configured decision tree, a developer wrote the branches in advance. Classify the request, follow the matching branch, and call the tools that branch names, in the order it names them.
  • In a model-driven loop, the developer provides tools and a goal. The model picks the next tool to call based on what the previous calls returned.

The exam favours model-driven decisions for agentic tasks, where the right sequence depends on what the agent discovers. It also expects you to know when deterministic control is still right. Later task statements build on that: 1.4 on enforcement, 1.5 on hooks.
a787f972f7:
The ticket comes from a wireless customer: "My bill went from $85 to $170 after I added a line, and the new phone you sent won't activate. Account A-30017."

Four tools are available: get_account, explain_bill_change, check_device_activation and resend_esim. Companion example 13_tree_vs_model.py runs both architectures on it.
c97a0d3980: Architecture A, the decision tree. A contact-centre routing layer typically looks like this. In a Spring service, you would write it with a classifier and a switch:
fbea042ecc:
Trace it. The lowercased ticket contains "bill", so the first branch fires. The tree calls explain_bill_change, formats the drivers, and returns: "Your bill rose from $85 to $170 because of: second line, Unlimited Plus, one-time activation fee, autopay discount removed."

The answer is accurate. It also answers only half the ticket. Nobody examined the activation problem. The tree chose its path once, from keywords, before gathering any data.

To fix it, you add a "bill AND activate" branch. Then someone writes in about a bill, a port-in and a lost phone, and you add another. This is the knowledge-acquisition bottleneck from section 02, alive in 2026.
9cb9fd708c: Architecture B, the model-driven loop. It has the same tools, a goal in the system prompt ("Resolve every issue in the ticket"), and the canonical loop. The trace:
25af186152:
Here is why each step happened.

  • Turn 1. The model sees two problems in the text. Both depend on account context (lines, plan, autopay status), so it fetches that first.
  • Turn 2. With the account in hand, the two investigations are independent. It requests both in one turn.
  • Turn 3. The activation result says BLOCKED, reason "eSIM profile not downloaded", fix "resend eSIM QR". The model decides to act on that. No branch anticipated this step.
  • Turn 4. It combines both findings. One detail came from turn 1: autopay was switched off. That detail makes the billing answer actionable.
8ec81f34c1:
The harness for B contains no business logic about bills or activations. That is both its strength and its risk.

The strength: it handles combinations nobody listed. It adapts its plan to intermediate results, such as the error in the refund trace or the activation fix here.

The risk: the path is not fixed in advance. You cannot read the code and know what will happen. That is why the next section of the exam guide (enforcement, hooks) exists.
c2922fe9ef:
Model-driven does not mean "never write control flow". It means: don't write control flow where the path depends on what the agent will discover.

Some decisions must be deterministic. The exam tests this boundary later in Domain 1:

  • a refund above a limit must never be issued without approval;
  • identity must be verified before account changes;
  • a regulated disclosure must always be shown.

Rely on the prompt alone for these, and you get a high probability, not a guarantee.

The pattern that combines both: the model decides what to try; code decides what is allowed. In the refund trace, the model chose to call issue_refund, and the tool (code) refused. Hooks and gating (task 1.5) generalise this. They intercept a tool call before it runs, and block or modify it by deterministic rules.
01f51a9bcb:
Here is a useful way to place a design on this spectrum.

  • A workflow is a pipeline where code calls the model at fixed points: classify, then extract, then summarise. The model fills in steps but does not choose them.
  • An agent is a loop in which the model chooses its next action and decides when it is finished.

Both are legitimate. The exam's 1.1 questions are about agents. Their wrong answers usually smuggle a workflow decision (a fixed tree, a fixed count) into the place where the model's decision belongs.
d6a9f1da7b: The task statement names three anti-patterns. All three replace the structured stop signal with something weaker. Each appears below as a broken implementation. It runs against a scripted model, so the failure is reproducible. The trace and the root cause follow.
35fcfc3f3c: The temptation: at the end of a task, the model writes "I'm done" or "Is there anything else I can help with?". So stop when you see those phrases. This is the ReAct-era Finish[...] habit, carried into an API that no longer needs it.
c1a6b6d34e:
Root cause. The first turn contained the word "done" in a subordinate clause ("once I'm done checking"). It also contained a tool_use block, and stop_reason was tool_use. The regex cannot tell intent from vocabulary.

The failure runs the other way too. A genuinely final answer may contain none of the keywords: "I wasn't able to locate that order, please check the number". The loop would call the model again. The model may then apologise again, and again.

Natural language is written for the customer. It changes with model versions, system prompts, languages and tone. The API sets stop_reason from what actually happened during generation. Fix: branch on stop_reason.
15cd489368: The temptation: loops are scary, so make the loop a for i in range(N). It always ends, which feels safe.
df8f3a065f:
Root cause. The refund needs five calls. The number 3 has no relation to the task. Someone picked it because it seemed enough.

On iteration 3, the model requested issue_refund, and the harness ran it, a side effect. Then the loop ended before the model could see the result, escalate, or tell the customer. The function returned an empty string with no error. The caller treats that as success.

Change the cap to 10 and this ticket works. The next ticket that needs 11 steps fails the same way. And a stuck model now burns 10 calls instead of 3 before failing silently.

A cap chosen as the termination condition is always either too small for some legitimate task or too large to protect you. Usually it is both.
0d2569090b:
Fix: stop_reason ends the loop. A budget exists as a circuit breaker that raises when exceeded (section 13).

Note what the caller sees in each case. The broken version returns ''. The fixed version with a tiny budget raises BudgetExceeded: no end_turn after 2 calls; escalate, do not return partial text.
440e37fb4b: The temptation: "if the model returned text, it is talking to the user, so it must be done". Variants include if response.content[0].type == "text" and if any(b.type == "text" ...). Another is if not any(b.type == "tool_use" ...), computed on a filtered or rebuilt list.
9c99b943cc:
Root cause. A response is an array of blocks. Text and tool calls coexist in one turn. Claude often writes a short preamble ("I'll start by pulling up the order.") before its tool_use blocks. So "has text" is true on most intermediate turns.

The check does three kinds of damage. It returns the preamble as the final answer. It leaves an unanswered tool_use in the history, so any later attempt to continue this conversation is a 400. And the customer receives a promise.

Fix: branch on stop_reason. Read text blocks only after deciding to exit.
70e4d6ae92:
If iteration caps are an anti-pattern, may an agent loop forever? No. The exam wording is precise. The anti-pattern is an arbitrary iteration cap as the primary stopping mechanism.

A loop still needs protection against runaway behaviour:

  • a model repeatedly calling the same failing tool;
  • a tool that returns something that triggers another call;
  • a prompt-injection in a tool result that sends the agent off course;
  • simply a very expensive task.

The difference lies in role and in behaviour.
d623101444: Role: stop_reason decides when the task is finished. The budget decides when something has gone wrong. A healthy run never reaches the budget.
fb56b4e183: Behaviour on trigger: when stop_reason ends the loop, you return the answer. When a budget trips, you raise. Mark the task failed or escalated, and keep the transcript for diagnosis. Never return the last text as if it were an answer.
d07add0a23: Size: set a budget well above the longest legitimate run you have seen, not at the length you expect. Say 3 to 5 times the 99th percentile of calls per task.
dc7c1a2cfb: Dimensions: count is only one. Tokens (cost), wall-clock time (latency SLO) and repetition (the same tool with the same input several times) catch failures that a count misses or catches late.
5cbab724c0:
The repetition detector caught the stuck run after three identical calls, long before the 20-call limit. That is the general lesson. A budget built around failure modes fires earlier, with a better diagnosis, than a single counter.

In Spring terms, this is a circuit breaker and a timeout around a remote call. You configure Resilience4j so a failing dependency does not take the service down. You don't use it to decide when a business process is complete.
9d3594470e: Once you have written the loop by hand, you notice that every team writes the same twenty lines. Two packaged versions exist, at different levels. For the exam, know that they are the same loop. Questions about the Agent SDK's max_turns or Claude Code's behaviour are questions about this chapter's mechanics.
c7e5677a63:
The Python and TypeScript client SDKs include a tool runner, a beta helper at the time of writing. You decorate plain functions. The decorator builds the JSON Schema from type hints and the docstring.

The runner then performs the loop. It calls the model. While the response asks for tools, it calls your functions, appends results, and calls again. It converts exceptions into is_error results.

Iterate over it to see each message, or call until_done() to get the last one. Companion example 16_sdk_tool_runner.py:
4ee4b24a41:
Its output is the same five-message trace as the hand-written loop, because it is the same loop. It generated a schema for lookup_order from the signature and docstring. That schema has "required": ["order_id"] and "additionalProperties": false, which is what you would have written by hand.

Use the runner when your tools are local functions and you want less code. Write the loop yourself when you need control over each step: custom persistence, approval gates, concurrency rules for side-effecting tools, or detailed per-turn telemetry. Either way, the same rules apply, including the meaning of max_iterations.
de3cbd9155:
The Claude Agent SDK packages the harness that powers Claude Code. It contains:

  • the loop;
  • built-in tools (file read and edit, shell, search);
  • permission modes;
  • hooks that run before and after tool calls;
  • automatic context compaction;
  • sessions that can be resumed;
  • subagents.

Your own tools reach it as MCP tools, either in-process or from external MCP servers. In Python:
9d623d3d10:
The stream of messages you receive is the history this chapter has built by hand. It has assistant messages with tool calls and user messages with tool results. A final result message records whether the run succeeded or stopped at a limit such as max_turns.

That last detail is the budgets-versus-caps lesson, built into the product. Hitting max_turns is reported as an error outcome, not as success.

The SDK's API surface moves faster than the protocol beneath it. Check its docs for exact option names when you build.
eb479944b1: Nothing in the protocol is Python-specific. The companion folder has two Java versions. One uses the Anthropic Java SDK. The other uses plain HTTP with Spring WebClient and Jackson. They are reference implementations for a Spring codebase. run_all.sh does not execute them, because they need dependencies on the classpath.
74331ea2c2:
The Java SDK (com.anthropic:anthropic-java) uses immutable params objects built with builders. One property suits a loop well. The MessageCreateParams.Builder can serve as the growing history. You add the assistant message and the tool results to the builder, and call build() for each request.

The snippet below targets the 2.x builder API. Method names sometimes move between releases. If one does not compile, check the SDK README for your version. The protocol it implements does not change.
d3a7bde6d2:
Line for line, it is the Python loop:

  • append the assistant turn (resp.toParam() converts the response into the request shape, keeping ids and any thinking blocks);
  • branch on the StopReason enum;
  • execute every ToolUseBlock;
  • add one user message with every ToolResultBlockParam;
  • fail loudly on anything unexpected.

Optional accessors (toolUse(), text()) replace Python's b.type == ... checks.
c5e79fd18f: Maybe you cannot add the SDK, or you want to see the wire format in a Spring service. Then the loop works directly on Jackson JsonNode trees. The messages array is an ArrayNode you append to. The response content array is copied into it untouched. That is the simplest way to guarantee that ids and signatures survive.
d8061fc6b5:
Three notes for a Spring deployment.

  • Blocking: .block() keeps the example readable. In a WebFlux service, express the loop as Mono.expand (each response expands into the next request until end_turn) or a recursive flatMap. On a servlet stack with Java 21, simply run the blocking loop on a virtual thread.
  • Parallel tools: run the tool_use blocks of one turn with CompletableFuture.allOf on a bounded executor. Then collect results in one ArrayNode.
  • Persistence: the history is just JSON. Store it per conversation in Redis or a JSONB column after each turn, and you get resumable agents. Persist the assistant turn and its tool results atomically. Then a crash never leaves an unanswered tool_use (section 06).
580f8333e2:
The model is non-deterministic. The loop must not be. Most loop bugs show up without a model at all: missed parallel results, text-based exits, lost assistant turns, unhandled stop reasons.

So test the loop against a scripted fake. It plays a fixed sequence of turns and validates every request the way the API would. The companion fake_client.py does this:

  • it returns real SDK Message objects, so loop code is identical in test and production;
  • it assigns tool_use ids;
  • it enforces the pairing and ordering rules with 400-style errors;
  • it estimates usage;
  • it records every request for assertions.
00da6aa984:
Each test pins one property from this chapter: termination ignores wording; pairing is complete; budgets raise; history is append-only. The other two in the companion file check two more things. Tool exceptions become is_error results. max_tokens is not treated as success.

The tests run in milliseconds and need no API key. They belong in CI next to your other unit tests.
e42e8e26c4:
The fake cannot test whether the model makes good choices. Does it call the right tool? Write good arguments? Escalate when it should? That needs evaluation against the real model, with recorded scenarios and graded outcomes. Later chapters cover it.

Keep the two separate: deterministic tests for the harness, evaluations for behaviour.

In a Spring project, the equivalent fake is a MockWebServer (OkHttp) or WireMock stub. It returns scripted JSON responses for successive POSTs to /v1/messages. It also lets you assert on the recorded request bodies.
1f1619471b: Someone will ask an agent that issued a refund "why?". With a decision tree, you read the code. With a model-driven loop, you read the trace, so the trace has to exist. The minimum useful record is one event per model call and one per tool execution, correlated by a run id:
4cb991f685:
Each field earns its place.

  • stop_reason per turn shows why the loop continued or ended. It makes the anti-patterns visible in production. A run whose final turn had stop_reason tool_use is a harness bug.
  • Tool names, ids and inputs show what the model chose. Redact personal data here, not later.
  • is_error and latency per tool show which dependency failed or slowed.
  • Tokens per turn feed the cost model of section 07 and the token budget of section 13.
  • The model's message id lets you correlate with provider-side logs.
77a3e14a01:
In a Spring shop, map this onto what you already run. Use one OpenTelemetry span per run. Add a child span per model call, with attributes for model, stop_reason and token counts. Add a child span per tool execution. Put the run id in the MDC, so application logs from inside tools join the same trace.

Useful dashboards follow directly:

  • distribution of turns per task (a shift upward after a prompt change is an early warning);
  • rate of budget trips;
  • rate of is_error per tool;
  • input tokens per task over time.

You can also persist the full messages array per run, with retention rules and redaction. Then you can replay any run against a new prompt or model version. That is the basis for regression evaluation.
ba0428409b: The CCAR-F exam presents scenarios with four options. For 1.1, the wrong options are usually plausible engineering ideas. They replace the structured signal or break the history. Work through each scenario before reading the reasoning.
45fbd34f79:
The symptom is the third anti-pattern: text content as completion indicator. The logs prove it, because text and tool_use arrived together. B replaces the check with the structured signal.

  • A tries to change model behaviour to fit a broken harness. It is probabilistic and does not fix the cause.
  • C is the first anti-pattern (natural-language parsing).
  • D addresses truncation. But the turn ended because of a tool call, not the token limit.
f50152f661:
The proposal makes an arbitrary cap the primary stop, the second anti-pattern. It also returns partial text as if it were an answer. Disputes needing six or seven calls would be cut off mid-investigation.

  • B keeps the same design with a different number. The next longer case fails the same way.
  • D overcorrects. A safety budget is legitimate protection against runaway loops.
  • C separates the two roles: stop_reason for completion, and a budget as a circuit breaker whose trigger is an error.
5f3a61fd04:
The harness answers only the first tool_use. The API requires a result for every tool_use id in the next message.

  • A misunderstands tool_choice. any forces the model to use a tool, not exactly one. The option that limits parallelism is disable_parallel_tool_use, and you would still need to answer every call.
  • C breaks pairing for whichever result each request leaves out.
  • D produces an orphaned tool_result, a different 400. It also loses the model's reasoning.
a32034181a:
Read the requirement: the path depends on what the agent discovers, and tickets carry several issues. That is the definition of where model-driven decision-making beats a pre-configured tree.

  • A grows the tree combinatorially.
  • B keeps the single up-front decision that caused the problem. A better classifier still picks one branch.
  • D wastes calls and still cannot act on findings, such as resending an eSIM after discovering the cause.
  • C also keeps deterministic enforcement where rules must always hold.
02d1870bbb:
The empty result tells the model the call succeeded, so it reports success. B gives the model accurate information, keeps the loop running, and lets it adapt. In this chapter's trace, it escalated.

  • A turns a recoverable business condition into a crash and a lost conversation.
  • C asks the model to guess about information the harness withheld.
  • D retries a deterministic business rejection, which will fail identically. Retries belong to transient errors inside the tool.
62363982a2:
Done when:

  • you can explain every line of the canonical loop;
  • you have seen each of the three anti-patterns fail and can name the root cause;
  • every pairing error in example 05 makes sense to you from the rules in section 06;
  • your new test fails if you reintroduce the content-check bug from example 11.
